questions.q: Name the year the Maoist insurgency began in Nepal and the leader of the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist) at that time.
questions.a: The insurgency began in 1996 under the leadership of Pushpa Kamal Dahal (Prachanda). A wrong answer (e.g., 2001 or Baburam Bhattarai) reveals confusion between the start of the armed struggle and later events like the royal massacre or the peace talks, indicating the student has not anchored the timeline correctly.

questions.q: Explain why King Gyanendra’s direct rule in February 2005 became a turning point that united the parliamentary parties and the Maoists against the monarchy.
questions.a: Gyanendra dismissed the elected government, assumed executive powers, and suspended civil liberties, exposing the monarchy as an obstacle to both democracy and a negotiated settlement. This pushed the Seven Party Alliance (SPA) and the Maoists to sign the 12-Point Understanding (Nov 2005), creating a united front. A wrong answer that focuses only on the Maoists’ military strength misses the political realignment that made the 2006 Jana Andolan possible.

questions.q: A Nepali citizen in 2007 reads that the Interim Constitution has declared Nepal a secular state. Using the concept of "popular sovereignty," analyze why this declaration was a direct consequence of the 2006 peace process.
questions.a: The 2006 Comprehensive Peace Agreement and the Interim Constitution transferred sovereignty from the king to the people, making the state’s identity (Hindu vs. secular) a matter of popular will rather than royal decree. The Maoists’ demand for a secular republic and the SPA’s acceptance reflected the new sovereign authority of the Constituent Assembly. A wrong answer that treats secularism as a mere policy change fails to link it to the fundamental shift in the locus of sovereignty.

questions.q: Compare the role of the Indian state in Nepal’s 2006 transition with its role in the 1950 Delhi Agreement. Identify one similarity and one key difference in India’s diplomatic approach.
questions.a: Similarity: India mediated between the monarchy and opposition forces in both cases. Difference: In 1950, India backed the Rana-monarchy compromise; in 2006, India facilitated the SPA-Maoist 12-Point Understanding, effectively sidelining the king. A wrong answer that claims India "imposed" the 2006 deal ignores the agency of Nepali actors and misreads India’s facilitative (not directive) role.

questions.q: Evaluate the argument: "The abolition of the monarchy in 2008 completed Nepal’s democratic transition." Provide two pieces of evidence supporting and two challenging this view.
questions.a: Supporting: (1) The Constituent Assembly’s first act was declaring a republic; (2) Elections to the CA were held with former combatants participating. Challenging: (1) The CA failed to promulgate a constitution until 2015 amid disputes over federalism; (2) Army integration and transitional justice remained unresolved. A wrong answer that gives only one side shows an inability to assess democratic consolidation as a process, not an event.

questions.q: Draft a three-point "Lessons Learned" memo for a peacebuilding practitioner, drawing on Nepal’s experience of integrating Maoist combatants into the national army (2006–2012).
questions.a: A strong memo includes: (1) Parallel political and military integration timelines prevent spoilers; (2) Verification of combatants by UNMIN (UN Mission in Nepal) built trust; (3) Delayed decisions on rank/rehabilitation fueled factionalism. A poor memo lists generic platitudes ("build trust") without referencing Nepal’s specific mechanisms (cantonment, verification, voluntary retirement packages).

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The Maoist Insurgency in Nepal (1996–2006) was a decade-long armed conflict launched by the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist) against the Hindu monarchy and the ______ system, aiming to establish a people's republic through protracted people's war.

Fill in the blank: Imagine a Class 12 student watching a ______ clip of Nepal’s 2008 Constituent Assembly session where the monarchy was abolished — a moment that transformed a Hindu kingdom into a secular republic.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain the socio-economic grievances that fueled the insurgency, trace the interplay between the Maoist armed struggle and the 2006 Jana Andolan (People's Movement), and evaluate the challenges of post-conflict transition including constitution-making, integration of combatants, and federal restructuring.
